g1: Picture the same cart with a small pull and a larger pull. Predict which pull changes its velocity faster.
g4: For the controlled lab, follow the transfer method later in the deck. Start with spare weights on the cart. Move them to the hanger so the whole moving mass stays fixed.
g5: Start from rest and check the velocity trace. A smooth rising line means the cart gained velocity. Use the same release point every time.
g6: Change the force that drives the system. Keep its total moving mass steady. Look for the change in acceleration.
g7: Yesterday you changed mass. Today you change force. Compare the two experiments to explain why both matter for the asteroid.
g8: Trace the velocity line in time order. Flat means zero acceleration. A falling line means negative acceleration. Use the velocity sign to describe how position changes.
g9: Recall the rule you tested with mass. Now reverse the experiment: keep the moving mass fixed and vary the net force.
g10: Read each force label and its predicted acceleration. These are model values. Look for what happens when the net force doubles.
g11: Draw a boundary around the cart, weights, and hanger. Ask whether a weight you add came from inside or outside that boundary.
g12: Compare the velocity change over the same time on both lines. A steeper line means a larger acceleration.
g13: Two versions are possible. Keeping only the cart’s mass fixed changes total mass as you add hanger weight. For the controlled run, transfer weight from the cart to the hanger.
g14: Before a trial, predict how moving one weight from cart to hanger will change the slope. Give a reason.
g15: Count all the moving pieces before and after the transfer. Their total mass is the same, but more weight now pulls downward on the hanging side.
g16: On your whiteboard draw one weight leaving the cart and the same weight arriving on the hanger. This shows what changes and what stays fixed.
g17: Choose force levels and plan repeated releases. Keep the track angle and starting point the same to make the comparison fair.
g18: Weigh the hanger in kilograms. Multiply its mass by gravity to get driving weight in newtons. Record the velocity slope separately.
g19: Choose the system before naming the force. The hanger’s weight drives the whole system. String tension pulls the cart and can differ from hanger weight.
g20: Fit a straight part of the velocity trace while the hanger falls. Record each slope with units and mark a failed release before trying again.
g21: Compare the full system before and after. If a weight comes from outside, both moving mass and driving force change.
g22: Read force across and acceleration up. For a graph against net force, slope is one divided by the mass of the system you chose. Hanger weight is only a proxy when resistance matters.
g23: Say both rules aloud: more force at fixed mass gives more acceleration; more mass at fixed force gives less acceleration. Connect them with the net-force equation.
g24: Divide the stated force by the asteroid’s mass. This estimates the acceleration due to that push. Time matters when estimating its effect on the path.
g25: These rows are calculated for constant total mass and negligible resistance. Label them as model data if you use them in Work.
g26: Put driving force along the bottom axis and acceleration on the side. Label both units. Compare the trend across trials instead of choosing just the neatest point.
g27: For acceleration plotted against net force, divide one by the slope to find mass. Check that the result is in kilograms.
g28: Compare the two net forces as a ratio. Use the same ratio for accelerations only if the mass stays fixed.
g29: Look back at both labs. Say what changed in each one, then use two values from today to support your claim.
g30: Work alone. Explain the effect of doubling net force at fixed mass. Then say what you would need to know before treating hanger weight as net force.
b1: The film holds cart mass fixed. Our controlled run holds the whole moving system fixed. Compare the two choices before you predict the result.
alt1: Students compare hanger weight with the tension pulling the cart.
b2: The film lists hanger weights beside cart accelerations. These weights are approximate pulling forces. Compare two rows without claiming they are your measurements.
alt2: Film sample table pairs hanger weights with accelerations of a fixed-mass cart.
b3: One lab varied mass. This lab varies force. The notebook combines both patterns to predict acceleration from net force and mass.
alt3: The notebook connects both labs to Newton’s second law.
b4: Maz gives her brother a careful answer. A push can change the path. Whether the change is enough depends on force, mass, time, and gravity.
alt4: Maz explains the asteroid prediction to her brother.
g2: Choose a slide lead and a scribe. Everyone predicts first and saves their own reasoning.
g3: Agree on who handles the equipment, checks safety, records readings, and checks the math. Share results after everyone has a job.
q1: How can you increase driving weight while keeping total moving mass fixed?
o1: Transfer a weight from cart to hanger.
o2: Add a new weight from the table to the hanger.
o3: Tilt the track more each time.
q2: Predict what doubling net force does to acceleration at fixed mass. Explain why adding a new weight to the hanger from outside the system would be a different test.
a2: At fixed mass, twice the net force gives twice the acceleration. Adding mass from outside also changes total moving mass.
q3: Record total moving mass. For each hanger setting, give its mass, driving weight in N, and your trial accelerations with units. Mark failed releases. If using supplied data, identify the source and record two rows with units.
q4: For one run, show how hanger mass in kg gives driving weight in N. Explain why this weight may differ from the tension on the cart or the net force on the whole system.
a4: Multiply hanger mass by gravity. An accelerating hanger can have tension different from its weight. Resistance can reduce the net driving force on the whole system.
q5: Use two force and acceleration rows from one source. Compare their ratios. Say how well they fit your prediction and name one limit of the comparison.
q6: Two systems have the same mass. One experiences twice the net force of the other. Compare their accelerations. Explain why doubling hanger weight in the film would not guarantee that exact result.
a6: Twice the net force gives twice the acceleration at fixed mass. In the film, hanger weight is a proxy, tension can differ, and adding hanger mass changes the whole moving mass.
p1a: Show a transfer of one weight from cart to hanger. Mark what stays fixed and what changes.
p1b: Sketch two velocity traces for the same total mass and different net forces. Explain your choice of slopes.
p2a: Choose a row. Calculate the hanger weight and identify which object or system you are describing.
p2b: Choose an acceleration. Explain how to get it from a straight velocity trace and how to check a bad release.
p3a: Compare two force levels. Say whether acceleration grew in about the same ratio and identify your data source.
p3b: Check your partner’s use of net force. Explain what the film can show about the trend and what it cannot prove exactly.

sample: Use the ideal table on the slides if you have no equipment. Record two force levels and accelerations with units. Label them as calculated data. The film uses a different setup; keep its rows separate.
discuss: Switch roles at the whiteboard. Compare one mass, slope, or assumption in each other’s explanation.
reply: Point to one value or line your classmate used. Explain what it supports or what needs a second look.
reflect: State one part of your explanation you checked or changed and why.
crit: Check the claim using a mass, a graph, or a trial. Give a corrected explanation.
solo: Work on your own. Give your prediction, critique the sample claim, and save your final reasoning.
